title: Singular Value Decomposition & Dimensionality Reduction
summary: SVD as the general matrix factorization and PCA as its headline application — the machinery behind embedding compression and recommenders.

slides.markdown:
Eigen-decomposition only works on square matrices. Most real data — a `users x items` ratings table, a `documents x words` matrix — isn't square. **SVD** factorizes *any* matrix, of any shape.

It's the single most reused piece of numerical linear algebra: PCA, recommenders, image compression, and pseudo-inverses all reduce to SVD underneath.

- SVD factors `A = UΣVᵀ` regardless of `A`'s shape.
- `Σ`'s diagonal (the singular values) ranks how much each "direction" of `A` matters.
- Keeping only the top few gives a compressed, low-rank approximation of `A`.

slides.subTitle: U, Σ, Vᵀ
slides.markdown:
`A = UΣVᵀ`: `U`'s columns are **left singular vectors** (orthonormal basis for the output space), `V`'s columns are **right singular vectors** (input space), and `Σ` is diagonal, holding the **singular values** — sorted largest to smallest.

![SVD factors any matrix into U, Sigma, and V transpose](assets/svd-factorization.svg)

Read it as: rotate the input (`Vᵀ`), stretch each axis by a singular value (`Σ`), rotate into the output space (`U`).

slides.subTitle: SVD vs eigen-decomposition
slides.markdown:
SVD generalizes eigen-decomposition rather than replacing it.

| | Eigen-decomposition | SVD |
|---|---|---|
| Requires square matrix | Yes | No |
| Guaranteed to exist | No (not always diagonalizable) | Yes, always |
| Relation | `M = PDP⁻¹` | `A = UΣVᵀ`; `U`, `V` are eigenvectors of `AAᵀ`, `AᵀA` |

In fact, the singular values of `A` are the square roots of the eigenvalues of `AᵀA` — SVD is eigen-decomposition applied to a related symmetric matrix, made to always work.

slides.subTitle: Keeping the top-k singular values
slides.markdown:
Singular values are sorted by importance — the first captures the most "structure" in `A`, the last the least. Truncating to the top `k` singular values (and their vectors) gives `A_k`, the **best possible rank-k approximation** of `A` in a precise mathematical sense (Eckart-Young theorem).

If `A` is `1000 x 1000` but only the top 20 singular values matter, you can store `A` using roughly `20*(1000+1000)` numbers instead of a million — a huge compression, with quantifiably bounded error.

This is the mechanism behind every "reduce to k dimensions" technique you'll use.

slides.subTitle: Variance-maximization intuition
slides.markdown:
**PCA** asks: what direction captures the most variance in the data? Center the data (subtract the mean), then run SVD on it — the right singular vectors (`V`) are exactly the **principal components**, and the singular values relate directly to how much variance each one explains.

So PCA doesn't need a separate algorithm; it's SVD applied to centered data, with the singular values telling you how many components to keep. (Area 12 `unsupervised-learning` covers PCA as an ML technique; this is the factorization underneath it.)

slides.subTitle: Recommender systems via matrix factorization
slides.markdown:
A `users x items` ratings matrix is huge and mostly empty (most users haven't rated most items). Factorizing it via (a variant of) SVD gives a low-rank approximation: each user and each item gets a short **latent vector**, and predicted rating = dot product of the two.

The compression is the point — instead of storing/learning every individual rating, you learn `k` latent factors per user and item (say `k=50`), and reconstruct any missing rating from them.

This was the core idea behind the winning Netflix Prize approaches.

slides.subTitle: Image compression via low-rank approximation
slides.markdown:
Treat a grayscale image as a matrix of pixel intensities. Most images are surprisingly low-rank in structure — large flat regions and repeated patterns mean a handful of singular values captures most of the visual content.

Keeping only the top `k` singular values reconstructs a visually close approximation using a fraction of the storage — `k=50` out of `500` singular values often looks nearly identical to the original, at roughly 10% the data.

This is a direct, visual demonstration of the same math powering recommenders and PCA.

slides.subTitle: Interpretability isn't free
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to think dimensionality reduction only "loses information" (boundable, acceptable). It also **loses interpretability** — a principal component is a *linear combination* of original features, not one you can label "income" or "age" anymore.

A reduced embedding might compress a user's behavior into 50 numbers that predict well, but none individually means anything explainable to a stakeholder or auditor.

When interpretability is a hard requirement (regulated decisions, debugging), factor that in before reaching for SVD/PCA — not just reconstruction error.

slides.subTitle: Rank-1 approximation by hand
slides.markdown:
`A = [[4, 0], [3, 0], [0, 5]]` (3x2). Its columns are already orthogonal-ish in structure: column 1 has norm `5` (from `[4,3]`), column 2 has norm `5` (from `[0,0,5]`), and the columns don't overlap in which rows are nonzero — so `A`'s singular values are exactly `σ1 = σ2 = 5`, with `U`, `V` picking out each column's direction.

```
A ≈ σ1 * u1 * v1ᵗ + σ2 * u2 * v2ᵗ
  = 5*[0.8,0.6,0]ᵗ*[1,0] + 5*[0,0,1]ᵗ*[0,1]
```

Keeping only the top term (`σ1=5`) gives a **rank-1 approximation** that reconstructs column 1 exactly and drops column 2 entirely — a concrete illustration of how truncating singular values trades exactness for compression, term by term, rather than as an abstract statement.
